chunks.text: Bounce probability by mobile page-load time, indexed against a one-second baseline. At 1 second: baseline reference. At 3 seconds: 32 percent higher bounce probability. At 6 seconds: 106 percent higher. At 10 seconds: 123 percent higher.
53% of mobile site visits are abandoned if a page takes longer than three seconds to load.
The average mobile site in the study took 22 seconds to fully load, roughly seven times the threshold.
Bounce probability rises sharply in the 3, 10 second range: a 3s load has a bounce probability 32% higher than a 1s load; at 6s it is 106% higher; at 10s it is 123% higher.
The study measured 11.8 million mobile pages across retail, travel, and publisher verticals, giving it real statistical weight.
Google's subsequent Core Web Vitals framework (twenty twenty onwards) codified the three-second threshold into the Largest Contentful Paint metric, where the "good" bucket ends at 2.5 seconds.
This is the anchor study behind every "mobile speed matters" claim in the library. It shows up in:

Why your restaurant loses reservations every night Leak number 1, slow mobile load, is grounded in this study. The 53% bounce rate is what makes the "lose half your traffic before the menu" framing real rather than rhetorical.

How much does a custom restaurant website cost? The performance-budget section of the pricing article points at this study to explain why a sub-two-second mobile load is treated as a baseline deliverable, not an upgrade.

Wix versus custom for restaurants: what breaks first Break number 2, the platform performance ceiling, references this study to explain why the three-second threshold is not reachable on most template builders without a rebuild.
